extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, lawmakers, and general readers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative dimensions Tocqueville uses to judge democratic vs aristocratic governments, and the civic effects of democratic institutions in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic laws promote the welfare of the greatest number
rubrics_metrics.description: “Democratic laws generally tend to promote the welfare of the greatest possible number; for they emanate from the majority of the citizens, who are subject to error, but who cannot have an interest opposed to their own advantage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville contrasts democracy with aristocracy: the purpose of democracy is useful to more people even if its means are imperfect. When evaluating laws, consider who they aim to benefit (majority vs minority) and whether the law's objective favors the greatest number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative expertise and efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Aristocracies are infinitely more expert in the science of legislation than democracies ever can be. ... Democracies, whose laws are almost always ineffective or inopportune.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the technical skill, coherence, and long‑term design in legislation: aristocracies often craft more deliberate, convergent legal programs; democracies may pass less expert, more ad hoc laws. Evaluate laws both for craftsmanship (means) and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish a law's ends from its means
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the consideration of laws a distinction must be carefully observed between the end at which they aim and the means by which they are directed to that end, between their absolute and their relative excellence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law can be well-drafted yet serve a bad purpose; conversely, a benevolent purpose poorly implemented may fail. When judging legislation, separately evaluate purpose (intended social goal) and effectiveness/efficiency of instruments used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to commit faults and to repair them (resilience)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us now imagine a community so organized by nature, or by its constitution, that it can support the transitory action of bad laws, and that it can await, without destruction, the general tendency of the legislation... the great advantage of the Americans consists in their being able to commit faults which they may afterward repair.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a polity's resilience: democracies may enact poor laws but can correct them over time; evaluate institutional mechanisms for self-correction and the community's ability to 'await' restorative trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of public officers' interests with the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the American democracy public officers have no permanent interests distinct from those of the majority—Result of this state of things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether officials' personal or caste interests diverge from the majority's interests. In democracies, officials' lack of permanent separate interests reduces incentives for long-term collusion against majority welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short tenure limits persistence of maladministration
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the democratic magistrate is more apt to misuse his power, he possesses it for a shorter period of time... The mal-administration of a democratic magistrate is a mere isolated fact, which only occurs during the short period for which he is elected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating harm from incompetence or corruption, factor in tenure length and turnover mechanisms: short terms localize harm and make systemic capture less likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic perpetuity and common interest create durable biases
rubrics_metrics.description: “The common purpose which connects the interest of the magistrates in aristocracies with that of a portion of their contemporaries identifies it with that of future generations; their influence belongs to the future as much as to the present.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocratic elites may form enduring collective interests that shape policy across generations; evaluate institutional durability and how continuing elite interests might bias legislation against the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of patriotism: instinctive versus reflective
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is one sort of patriotic attachment which principally arises from that instinctive, disinterested, and undefinable feeling... But there is another species of attachment to a country which is more rational... it is nourished by the laws, it grows by the exercise of civil rights, and, in the end, it is confounded with the personal interest of the citizen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between instinctive (emotional, tradition‑based) patriotism and reflective (reasoned, rights‑based) patriotism. Reflective patriotism is more durable and productive of continuous civic effort; evaluate which predominates and the consequences for sustained public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending political rights to foster civic interest
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most powerful, and perhaps the only, means of interesting men in the welfare of their country which we still possess is to make them partakers in the Government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reforms or institutional designs by their capacity to enfranchise and involve citizens: giving people a role in government increases civic zeal and aligns private with public interests, though timing and readiness of the populace matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise of rights teaches respect for rights
rubrics_metrics.description: “The only means... of inculcating the notion of rights, and of rendering it, as it were, palpable to the senses, is to invest all the members of the community with the peaceful exercise of certain rights... When a child... he has no notion of the property of others; but as he gradually learns the value of things... he observes those rights in others which he wishes to have respected in himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights are best learned by practice: evaluate whether citizens actually exercise property and political rights, since practical engagement fosters mutual respect and reduces anti‑property sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of law increased by popular origin and personal stake
rubrics_metrics.description: “This popular origin... contributes prodigiously to increase its power. ... everyone is personally interested in enforcing the obedience of the whole community to the law; for as the minority may shortly rally the majority to its principles, it is interested in professing that respect for the decrees of the legislator which it may soon have occasion to claim for its own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws that are seen as emanating from the people and in which individuals have a stake are more likely to be obeyed. Evaluate legitimacy sources (popular origin, personal interest) when judging compliance and respect for law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic political activity pervades society and drives progress
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cares of political life engross a most prominent place in the occupation of a citizen in the United States... The great political agitation of the American legislative bodies... is a mere episode or a sort of continuation of that universal movement which originates in the lowest classes of the people and extends successively to all the ranks of society.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of civic mobilization and grassroots organizational life (town meetings, societies, debates). Broad civic activity correlates with social improvement and commercial dynamism; Tocqueville gives examples like temperance societies and local improvement meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic defects are immediately visible; advantages require long observation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The defects and the weaknesses of a democratic government may very readily be discovered; they are demonstrated by the most flagrant instances, whilst its beneficial influence is less perceptibly exercised... A single glance suffices to detect its evil consequences, but its good qualities can only be discerned by long observation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing democratic regimes, be cautious of snap judgments: short‑term scandals or legislative errors are salient, while long‑term benefits (resilience, broad welfare) may be less visible and require longitudinal study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy favors the greatest number, not all classes
rubrics_metrics.description: “The advantage of democracy does not consist, therefore, as has sometimes been asserted, in favoring the prosperity of all, but simply in contributing to the well‑being of the greatest possible number.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate distributive effects: democracies tend to protect and promote majority interests and may neglect or harm minority or elite interests. Recognize this as a structural feature rather than a simple failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of aligning rulers' interests with community welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is perhaps still more important that the interests of those men should not differ from the interests of the community at large; for, if such were the case, virtues of a high order might become useless, and talents might be turned to a bad account.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing leadership, prioritize alignment of incentives between rulers and the public over merely measuring individual virtue or talent; misaligned interests can subvert otherwise admirable capacities.
